questions.q: What is a Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule template?
options: A blank KQL editor with no pre-filled logic at all
A feature exclusive to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, unrelated to Sentinel
A rule that can only be used once and then must be deleted
A pre-built rule Microsoft ships with its query, schedule, severity, and mapping already filled in
questions.explain: Templates are authored and maintained by Microsoft's security research teams, with the query and settings ready to enable.

questions.q: What is usually the one thing you need to supply before a built-in template starts producing alerts?
options: The matching data connector, turned on and feeding the workspace
A separate Azure subscription dedicated to that rule
A brand-new Log Analytics workspace just for that template
A custom KQL query written from scratch
questions.explain: A template built for a given data source returns no results if that connector isn't enabled and sending data.

questions.q: When is a custom analytics rule the only real option?
options: Whenever you want faster time-to-value than a template could offer
Custom rules are never actually necessary
Only when Microsoft has deprecated every available template
When the logic is specific to your own environment, such as a custom app's log table or an org-specific business rule
questions.explain: No vendor template can anticipate logic that only applies to one organization's own systems or policies.

questions.q: What is the real cost of choosing a custom rule over a built-in template?
options: Custom rules cannot generate incidents under any circumstances
Custom rules always run slower than built-in templates
You own the query's correctness and all future tuning, with no Microsoft-maintained updates
There is no cost difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: Unlike a template, nobody at Microsoft updates a custom rule as the environment or data source changes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how do most real Sentinel deployments actually use built-in and custom rules?
options: They rely exclusively on custom rules and never enable any template
They disable all built-in templates immediately after deployment
They run a mix: templates for common, well-understood threats and custom rules for the handful of things unique to that organization
They rely exclusively on templates and never write a custom rule
questions.explain: Neither option is categorically better; most deployments combine fast, vetted coverage with targeted custom logic.
